newsitem.title: ITALY: Exiled Cubans count on Pope in meeting with Castro.
newsitem.headline: Exiled Cubans count on Pope in meeting with Castro.

text.p: Cuban exiles said on Sunday they were counting on Pope John Paul to tell communist President Fidel Castro to end human rights abuses and open the door to democracy at an historic Vatican meeting this week.
About 80 Cubans, most of whom live in Miami, braved torrential rain to listen to the Pontiff's weekly angelus address in St Peter's Square.
"John Paul, friend, Cuba is counting on you," read a huge banner. Another read: "Holy Father, Cuban exiles trust you."
The Vatican ended weeks of speculation on Saturday when it announced that Castro, who has ruled the Caribbean island for nearly 38 years, would have an audience with the Pope.

The meeting between one of Marxism's great survivors and the Pontiff, acknowledged as a key influence in the collapse of communism in his native Poland and elsewhere in eastern Europe, will take place on Tuesday.

Castro, who came to Rome for a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit, said on Saturday that he expected the meeting "will be positive". But the exiles said they hoped it would be a prelude to the downfall of the 70-year-old revolutionary.
"Every time the Pope hugs a dictator, it means that person will fall. I have no doubts it (the meeting) will help," said Miguel Angel Loredo, a Franciscan monk living in New York.

"It's the beginning of something that will end in the freedom of Cuba...Castro is a tool the Pope has to use to open the door," said Loredo, who said he had been imprisoned by Castro for 10 years on "fabricated charges".
"Everything Fidel Castro says is false, it's lies," said Mario Chanas de Armas, another former prisoner.
"How can you believe a murderer, a man who has enslaved his people? A man who has shot who knows how many thousands of men?"
Chanas de Armas said people would not have a romantic notion of Castro as an revolutionary hero if they had to live with food rationing and state-controlled media.
"Then they'll have real communism like we have in Cuba," he said.

Castro, taught as a child by Jesuit priests, caused a sensation at the food summit with a passionate anti-capitalist tirade that equated hunger with genocide and branded a 34-year-old U.S. trade embargo "criminal" and "absurd".
"The rich do not know hunger," he said in a loudly-applauded speech on Saturday.
"It is capitalism, neoliberalism, the laws of a wild market, the external debt, underdevelopment and the unequal terms of reference that are killing so many people in the world."

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi told Castro on Saturday that there was a lot of truth in the hard-hitting speech but Emma Bonino, the European Humanitarian Affairs Commissioner, said she was "stupefied" by the warmth of Castro's reception.

The harshest criticism of Castro at the summit came from Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, who told a news conference he would work to boost ties between Cuba and the European Union provided "Cuba shows signs of democracy".
"It no longer depends on me, or on the EU," Aznar said.
